Optimizing Retrieval Components for a Shared Backbone via Component-Wise Multi-Stage Training

CCS: Computing methodologies Information retrievalCCS: Computing methodologies RankingCCS: Information systems Enterprise information systemsCCS: Information systems Search engine architectures and scalability
Yunhan Li Note: Both authors contributed equally to this research. Affiliation: Deli Joint Laboratory, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China Affiliation: City University of Macau, Macau, Macau, Macau email: D24092110205@cityu.edu.mo , Mingjie Xie Affiliation: Deli Joint Laboratory, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China email: suat25060313@stu.suat-sz.edu.cn , Zihan Gong Affiliation: Deli Joint Laboratory, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China , Zeyang Shi Affiliation: Deli Joint Laboratory, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China , Gengshen Wu Note: Corresponding author. Affiliation: City University of Macau, Macau, Macau, Macau email: gswu@cityu.edu.mo and Min Yang Affiliation: Deli Joint Laboratory, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China email: min.yang@siat.ac.cn
Abstract.

Recent advances in embedding-based retrieval have enabled dense retrievers to serve as core infrastructure in many industrial systems, where a single retrieval backbone is often shared across multiple downstream applications. In such settings, retrieval quality directly constrains system performance and extensibility, while coupling model selection, deployment, and rollback decisions across applications.

In this paper, we present empirical findings and a system-level solution for optimizing retrieval components deployed as a shared backbone in production legal retrieval systems. We adopt a multi-stage optimization framework for dense retrievers and rerankers, and show that different retrieval components exhibit stage-dependent trade-offs. These observations motivate a component-wise, mixed-stage configuration rather than relying on a single uniformly optimal checkpoint. The resulting backbone is validated through end-to-end evaluation and deployed as a shared retrieval service supporting multiple industrial applications.

Keywords: 
Information Retrieval, Legal Search, Dense Retrieval, Curriculum Learning

1. Introduction

In practice, legal AI systems increasingly rely on retrieval services as a shared foundation that connects heterogeneous legal data sources with a wide range of downstream applications (Armour and Sako, 2020; Stavropoulou et al., 2020). In such systems, retrieval is no longer a task-specific component, but a core infrastructure whose quality directly impacts the effectiveness, stability, and extensibility of all dependent capabilities. Consequently, limitations in retrieval accuracy or ranking quality are propagated across the entire system, making optimization of retrieval backbones deployed in shared settings a critical problem in practical deployments.

This shared-backbone setting arises naturally in real-world legal AI products. In our production environment, the legal retrieval system is designed as a foundational infrastructure underlying multiple product modules, rather than serving isolated application scenarios. In the production legal AI system operated at Deli, a unified retrieval service supports diverse downstream applications, including the Deli legal services platform and other internal legal workflows. As illustrated in Figure 1, a single retrieval layer simultaneously serves heterogeneous interaction modes under shared deployment constraints. Maintaining separate retrieval checkpoints for individual applications is impractical in this setting, as it would substantially increase deployment and monitoring complexity, failure recovery cost, as well as the ongoing burden of data curation and model updates driven by newly observed user feedback and failure cases. As a result, the retrieval backbone defines the performance ceiling of existing applications and constrains the extensibility of future retrieval-dependent services.

Despite recent advances in open-source embedding and reranking models for dense retrieval (Zhao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), optimizing retrieval backbones for legal AI systems remains challenging in practice. Legal retrieval involves domain-specific terminology, subtle semantic distinctions between legally related concepts, and informal expressions common in real-world legal workflows (Bajčić, 2017; Maxwell and Schafer, 2008). General-purpose retrieval models trained on open-domain corpora often struggle to accurately capture such relevance signals (Li et al., 2026), and these limitations are further amplified when deployed as a shared backbone.

In this work, we investigate how to optimize shared retrieval backbones under real-world deployment constraints. We focus on the retrieval layer rather than application-specific or end-to-end tuning, and adopt a staged training framework with progressively harder supervision. Experiments on production legal retrieval workloads with real user queries reveal stage-dependent behaviors of embedding and reranking models, leading to practical insights for component-level optimization and model selection. We release our trained models to support reproducibility.

2. Unified Multi-Stage Training Methodology

Our production retrieval systems operate under a shared-model setting, where a single retrieval model family is deployed across multiple legal information access scenarios. As introduced in Section 1, these scenarios include direct statute retrieval, retrieval components within retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)–based legal analysis systems (Lewis et al., 2020), and other retrieval-dependent applications. In such an environment, maintaining separate models for individual tasks is impractical due to deployment complexity, maintenance cost, and stability requirements. We therefore adopt a unified training strategy that incrementally refines the same retrieval model through multiple stages (Zhang et al., 2025), drawing inspiration from curriculum learning (Bengio et al., 2009) by progressively introducing training signals of increasing difficulty, rather than optimizing task-specific models in isolation. This multi-stage training strategy is applied consistently to both embedding-based retrievers and rerankers within our retrieval system.

Rather than relying on a single training objective or dataset, our approach adopts a curriculum-style multi-stage refinement process, inspired by prior work on domain-adaptive retrieval training (Hao et al., 2025). Each stage emphasizes a different aspect of retrieval quality, with supervision progressing from broad semantic alignment to fine-grained relevance discrimination and robustness calibration.

Importantly, the stages are not intended to form a strictly monotonic optimization path toward a single objective. Instead, later stages may improve certain system metrics while degrading others, revealing explicit trade-offs across retrieval objectives. The multi-stage framework therefore serves as an empirical exploration of stage-dependent training behaviors, enabling different retrieval components to benefit from different stages rather than assuming a single uniformly optimal checkpoint. An overview of the multi-stage training pipeline is shown in Figure 2.

The first stage establishes broad semantic alignment between queries and legal texts using large-scale heterogeneous weak supervision collected from multiple sources, including curated data, domain literature, real-world cases, and synthetic queries. This stage emphasizes representation coverage and generalization, optimizing for coarse-grained semantic recall rather than fine-grained ranking accuracy (Wen et al., 2024).

Building on Stage 1, the second stage focuses on relevance refinement through automatically mined hard samples, corresponding to instances where the model exhibits suboptimal retrieval behavior (Nian et al., 2025). By repeatedly training on such hard cases, Stage 2 improves sensitivity to fine-grained relevance differences, which is critical for user-facing retrieval and ranking scenarios.

The third stage targets robustness under semantically ambiguous and high-risk queries. Training relies on more selective, high-quality query sources and dynamically mined challenging negatives that are refreshed at each epoch based on the current model state. This stage functions as a calibration step to enhance robustness, rather than guaranteeing uniform improvements across all retrieval metrics.

Across all stages, the same retrieval model family is incrementally refined. Model selection and evaluation are guided by the functional role of each retrieval component rather than the training stage itself, reflecting the distinct objectives of coverage-oriented retrieval and fine-grained relevance ranking.

3. Evaluation and Analysis

3.1. Evaluation Setup and Datasets

We evaluate our retrieval models on two Chinese legal question answering benchmarks with complementary characteristics. Unless otherwise specified, we use Qwen3-Embedding-4B and Qwen3-Reranker-4B (Zhang et al., 2025) as the shared baseline models (denoted as Base) for all embedding and reranking evaluations.

CSAID (Li et al., 2026), is a legal question answering benchmark derived from real-world application workflows and reflects complex, context-rich information needs, as described in prior work.

STARD (Su et al., 2024), is a standardized Chinese statute retrieval benchmark derived from real-life legal consultation queries issued by non-professional users. It captures diverse and informal information needs that lack precise legal terminology, and is used in our evaluation to assess generalization under controlled retrieval settings.

Our evaluation follows a shared retrieval setting in which a unified retrieval system serves multiple downstream applications. We report Recall@K for embedding models to measure candidate coverage (Chang et al., 2020), and ranking-sensitive metrics such as MRR and nDCG for reranking models to capture ordering quality. All metrics are computed under a consistent evaluation protocol unless otherwise specified.

3.2. Component-Level Analysis and Findings

Figure 3 illustrates recall as a function of retrieval budget across different training stages, while Table 1 reports recall at representative cutoff values on CSAID and STARD. Across both benchmarks, later training stages consistently achieve higher recall under the same retrieval budgets, indicating progressively improved candidate coverage at the embedding level.

On CSAID, which reflects application-driven and context-rich queries, Stage 3 yields the strongest recall across all reported K values. Similar improvements are observed on STARD, where Stage 3 also achieves the highest recall, suggesting that recall gains on practical workloads do not come at the expense of generalization to standardized statute retrieval. Taken together, the recall–budget curves indicate that later-stage embedding models can reach comparable recall targets with substantially smaller retrieval budgets. From a system perspective, this enables reductions in the number of retrieved candidates in latency-sensitive configurations, thereby lowering downstream reranking cost while maintaining retrieval coverage. The system-level implications of these recall–budget trade-offs are discussed in Section 3.5.

In contrast to embeddings, reranking performance exhibits clear stage-dependent trade-offs. Table 2 reports reranking performance on CSAID and STARD in terms of MRR and nDCG. We compare our multi-stage trained rerankers against widely used open-source baselines, as well as a shared-base reranker trained under different stages. Overall, reranking performance consistently improves with task-specific fine-tuning, substantially outperforming generic reranker models across both benchmarks.

On CSAID, Stage 2 achieves the strongest overall ranking quality, yielding the highest MRR and nDCG, while Stage 3 delivers comparable performance with marginal differences. On STARD, Stage 3 slightly outperforms other stages in both metrics, suggesting improved generalization to standardized statute retrieval queries. Taken together, these results indicate that reranking quality does not improve monotonically across training stages. Later-stage training signals may improve certain objectives, such as robustness or generalization, while slightly degrading fine-grained relevance alignment required for user-facing ranking, thereby forcing explicit trade-offs in reranker model selection.

3.3. Model Selection and RAG Evaluation

Based on the component-level results in Sections 3.2 and 3.3, we adopt a mixed-stage configuration for end-to-end evaluation, combining the Stage 3 embedding model with the Stage 2 reranker (denoted as our in Table 3). This configuration aligns with the complementary roles of the two components, where embeddings primarily affect candidate coverage across retrieval budgets, while rerankers are more sensitive to in-domain relevance.

As shown in Table 3, this mixed-stage setup consistently improves end-to-end retrieval performance on both CSAID and STARD over the shared baseline (Base) using Qwen3-Embedding-4B and Qwen3-Reranker-4B without multi-stage fine-tuning. These results support component-wise model selection as a practical deployment choice and motivate the deployment considerations discussed next.

3.4. System-Level Trade-offs

The recall–budget trends in Figure 3 provide concrete guidance for configuring retrieval systems under different application requirements, highlighting the need to balance latency constraints and retrieval quality rather than adopting a single uniform setting.

In latency-sensitive scenarios such as high-frequency API-based retrieval, later-stage embeddings achieve comparable recall with substantially smaller retrieval budgets, allowing the system to reduce the number of retrieved candidates while maintaining the same recall target and lowering reranking computation and end-to-end latency. For general legal search applications that balance efficiency and result quality, moderate retrieval budgets can effectively leverage both improved embedding coverage and reranking effectiveness, yielding stronger candidate sets without increasing system cost. In performance-oriented scenarios such as in-depth legal research and analysis, larger retrieval budgets can be employed when latency constraints are relaxed, enabling reranking models to operate on richer candidate sets and maximizing overall retrieval quality.

Together, these observations demonstrate that the primary value of multi-stage training lies in enabling flexible, application-specific retrieval configurations, where different components and operating points can be selected based on system-level trade-offs rather than a single globally optimal setting.

Overall, these observations highlight that the primary value of multi-stage training lies in enabling flexible, application-specific system configurations. Different components may reach their optimal operating points at different stages, and practical deployment benefits from selecting and combining models based on system-level trade-offs rather than relying on a single globally optimal checkpoint.

3.5. Offline A/B Test

We conduct a lightweight offline A/B test to assess deployment readiness in a realistic production setting. A total of 389 real user queries from two independent application datasets are evaluated using end-to-end RAG responses generated with the base and improved retrieval backbones under identical generation settings. For queries with identical retrieved results, no preference is recorded; otherwise, responses are judged in a double-blind manner with randomized positions. Across both datasets, the improved backbone is preferred in 173 cases, compared to 144 for the base system, with 72 ties. Excluding ties, the improved system is preferred in 54.6% of comparisons, indicating a consistent directional improvement aligned with the retrieval gains reported earlier. This evaluation serves as a deployment sanity check rather than a hypothesis-testing benchmark.

In terms of efficiency, the improved backbone processes 389 queries in 10 minutes and 18 seconds, compared to 9 minutes and 39 seconds for the base system, incurring an additional cost of 39 seconds overall. This corresponds to an average overhead of approximately 0.10 seconds per query (6.7% relative increase), mainly due to stacking multiple LoRA adapters across training stages. Given the modest overhead and consistent quality gains, the proposed backbone has been deployed in production as a shared retrieval infrastructure for multiple RAG-based legal applications.

4. Conclusion

We present a multi-stage training framework for retrieval components deployed as a unified backbone in industrial legal retrieval systems. Our results show that embedding and reranking components benefit from different training stages, and suggest that, in shared retrieval settings, role-aware component selection can be more effective than relying on a single uniformly chosen checkpoint. These findings highlight that multi-stage training supports flexible, deployment-oriented retrieval configurations under diverse latency and quality constraints.
